label: Introduction to Ergodic Theory
notes: Open by framing ergodic theory as the statistical face of Hamiltonian mechanics. We cannot integrate most systems explicitly, so instead we ask what fraction of time an orbit spends in a region. The energy surface carries an invariant measure, and that measure is the bridge from individual trajectories to long-run averages.

label: Measure-Preserving Systems
notes: Define the abstract object carefully: a probability space together with a transformation or flow that leaves the measure invariant. Stress that invariance means preimages of a set have the same measure as the set, which is the natural language for both discrete maps and continuous flows on phase space.

label: The Liouville Measure
notes: Connect the abstraction to mechanics. Liouville's theorem says the Hamiltonian flow preserves phase volume, and restricting to a fixed energy level gives a finite invariant measure once we divide by the gradient of the energy. Emphasize that this is the canonical invariant measure ergodic theory acts upon here.

label: Poincare Recurrence
notes: Walk through the pigeonhole argument. If a positive-measure set never returned, its forward iterates would be disjoint and consume infinite measure, contradicting finiteness. Conclude that almost every point returns arbitrarily near its start. Highlight the apparent paradox with irreversibility and resolve it by recurrence times being astronomically long.

label: Ergodicity
notes: Introduce ergodicity as indecomposability: no invariant set splits the space into two parts of positive measure. Equivalently, invariant functions are constant almost everywhere. Contrast an ergodic system, whose typical orbit explores the whole energy surface, with a decomposable one that stays trapped in a sub-region forever.

label: Birkhoff's Ergodic Theorem
notes: State the central theorem precisely. Time averages along an orbit converge for almost every initial point. When the system is ergodic the limit is constant and equals the space average. This is the rigorous statement of the physicist's hope that time spent equals phase volume occupied.

label: Time Average Equals Space Average
notes: This is the visual heart of the lecture. Show a single trajectory winding densely over the energy surface and argue that the proportion of time near any region matches that region's measure. Stress almost every: a measure-zero set of exceptional initial conditions may behave differently, and that caveat is essential.

label: Mixing
notes: Define mixing as asymptotic independence: the measure of the intersection of a moved set with a fixed set factorizes in the limit. Explain that mixing implies ergodicity but is strictly stronger, describing systems that forget their initial conditions and spread any blob uniformly across the whole space.

label: Rotations and Torus Translations
notes: Present the simplest examples. An irrational rotation of the circle is ergodic but not mixing; orbits equidistribute yet rigidly preserve spacing. The irrational translation on the torus generalizes this. Use Weyl equidistribution to make the connection between number theory and ergodicity concrete and memorable.

label: Geodesic Flow on Negative Curvature
notes: Contrast the rotations with the geodesic flow on a surface of negative curvature. Here nearby geodesics diverge exponentially, producing genuine mixing and strong chaos. This is the canonical mechanical example where the energy surface is explored thoroughly and sensitive dependence reigns. It motivates the leap from order to chaos.

label: Recurrence Under Volume Preservation
notes: Return to recurrence with a concrete picture: a droplet of phase points carried by the volume-preserving flow must eventually overlap its starting region. Tie this to the measure-theoretic proof and to the physical intuition that incompressible flow on a finite-volume surface cannot escape to infinity, forcing return.

label: Synthesis and Outlook
notes: Close by assembling the hierarchy: measure preservation gives recurrence, ergodicity gives equality of averages, mixing gives decay of correlations. Remind students that these properties justify statistical mechanics' replacement of intractable trajectories by averages, and point ahead to entropy and the deeper classification of dynamical systems.
